# Loading the relational database


```{r load-db}
normalized_dir <- "Data/Normalized"
table_order <- c("COMPANY", "JOB_POSTING", "SALARY", "SKILL", "JOB_SKILL")

if (params$db_backend == "postgres") {
  con <- dbConnect(
    RPostgres::Postgres(),
    dbname = "data607_project3", host = "localhost", port = 5432,
    user = "postgres", password = Sys.getenv("PGPASSWORD")
  )
} else {
  con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
  dbExecute(con, "PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;")

  # Reuse the team's PostgreSQL DDL; SQLite accepts the same column types
  ddl <- read_file("SQL guide/Dataset1_Create_Tables.sql") %>%
    str_remove_all("(?m)--.*$") %>%
    str_replace_all("public\\.", "") %>%
    str_split(";") %>% unlist() %>% str_trim()
  walk(ddl[ddl != ""], ~ dbExecute(con, .x))

  # Load parents before children so every foreign key is checked on insert
  for (tbl in table_order) {
    df <- read_csv(file.path(normalized_dir, paste0(tbl, ".csv")),
                   show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
      mutate(across(where(is.POSIXct), ~ format(.x, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")),
             across(where(is.logical), as.integer))
    dbAppendTable(con, str_to_lower(tbl), df)
  }
}

dbListTables(con)
```

Long job–skill table:

```{r db-query}
jobs <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT j.job_id, c.company_name, j.title, j.department, j.city, j.region,
         j.country_code, j.workplace_type, j.employment_type, j.seniority,
         j.posted_at, j.description, j.job_category_updated AS job_category,
         s.salary_currency, s.salary_period, s.salary_min_annual,
         s.salary_max_annual, s.salary_midpoint_annual, s.salary_valid,
         s.salary_outlier_flag, s.salary_usd_eligible
  FROM job_posting j
  JOIN company c ON c.company_id = j.company_id
  LEFT JOIN salary s ON s.job_id = j.job_id
") %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(across(c(salary_valid, salary_outlier_flag, salary_usd_eligible),
                ~ as.logical(as.integer(.x))),
         posted_at = as.POSIXct(posted_at, tz = "UTC"))

skills_db <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT js.job_id, k.skill_id, k.skill_name
  FROM job_skill js
  JOIN skill k ON k.skill_id = js.skill_id
") %>% as_tibble()

skill_catalog <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM skill ORDER BY skill_id") %>%
  as_tibble()

dbDisconnect(con)

glimpse(jobs)
```

```{r salary-quality}
salary_status <- jobs %>%
  mutate(status = case_when(
    is.na(salary_currency)              ~ "No salary advertised",
    salary_currency != "USD"            ~ "Non-USD currency",
    !salary_valid %in% TRUE             ~ "Invalid or incomplete range",
    salary_outlier_flag                 ~ "Outlier flag (< $30K or > $400K)",
    salary_usd_eligible                 ~ "USD-eligible (used for pay analysis)",
    TRUE                                ~ "Other"
  )) %>%
  count(status, sort = TRUE)

salary_status %>% kbl_style(caption = "Salary status of the 226 data-role postings")

pay <- jobs %>% filter(salary_usd_eligible)
q   <- quantile(pay$salary_midpoint_annual, c(.25, .75))
iqr_fence <- c(q[1] - 1.5 * diff(q), q[2] + 1.5 * diff(q))
pay <- pay %>%
  mutate(range_ratio = salary_max_annual / salary_min_annual,
         iqr_outlier = salary_midpoint_annual < iqr_fence[1] |
                       salary_midpoint_annual > iqr_fence[2])
```



# Value Proxy 1: Demand

```{r demand}
n_jobs <- nrow(jobs)

wilson <- function(x, n, z = 1.96) {
  p <- x / n
  centre <- (p + z^2 / (2 * n)) / (1 + z^2 / n)
  half   <- z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2)) / (1 + z^2 / n)
  tibble(lo = centre - half, hi = centre + half)
}

demand <- skills %>%
  count(skill_name,name = "postings") %>%
  mutate(share = postings / n_jobs) %>%
  bind_cols(wilson(.$postings, n_jobs)) %>%
  arrange(desc(share)) %>%
  mutate(demand_rank = row_number())

write_csv(demand, "Data/Analysis/skill_demand.csv")
```

```{r demand-plot, fig.height = 7.5}
ggplot(demand, aes(share, fct_reorder(skill_name, share))) +
  geom_col(fill = col_main, width = 0.72) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.3, colour = "#52514e",
                 linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_text(aes(x = hi, label = pct(share, 1)), hjust = -0.25, size = 3.1,
            colour = "#52514e") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))) +
  labs(title = "Share of data-role postings that mention each skill",
       subtitle = paste0(n_jobs, " postings; whiskers are 95% Wilson confidence intervals"),
       x = "Share of postings", y = NULL)
```

**Findings:**

* **Python (`r pct(demand$share[demand$skill_name == "Python"])`) and SQL
  (`r pct(demand$share[demand$skill_name == "SQL"])`)** 
* The next tier is **Machine Learning, LLMs, Statistics, Data Pipelines, dbt
  and AWS**, each mentioned in roughly a fifth to a third of postings.
* **R** is mentioned in only `r pct(demand$share[demand$skill_name == "R"])`
  of postings...

## How many skills does a posting ask for?

```{r breadth, fig.height = 4}
skills_per_job <- jobs %>%
  select(job_id, job_category) %>%
  left_join(count(skills, job_id, name = "n_skills"), by = "job_id") %>%
  mutate(n_skills = coalesce(n_skills, 0L))

ggplot(skills_per_job, aes(n_skills)) +
  geom_bar(fill = col_main, width = 0.75) +
  labs(title = "Number of tracked skills mentioned per posting",
       subtitle = paste0("Median ", median(skills_per_job$n_skills),
                         "; ", sum(skills_per_job$n_skills == 0),
                         " postings mention none of the 30 tracked skills"),
       x = "Skills mentioned", y = "Postings")
```

A typical posting names about `r median(skills_per_job$n_skills)` of our 30
skills. Employers usually ask for a **bundle** of skills, not a single tool, so
Section 5 looks at which skills appear together.

## Demand differs by role

```{r demand-category, fig.height = 7.5}
cat_n <- count(jobs, job_category, name = "cat_jobs")

top_skills <- demand %>% slice_head(n = 18) %>% pull(skill_name)

by_cat <- skills %>%
  left_join(select(jobs, job_id, job_category), by = "job_id") %>%
  count(job_category, skill_name) %>%
  right_join(expand_grid(job_category = cat_n$job_category, skill_name = top_skills),
             by = c("job_category", "skill_name")) %>%
  mutate(n = coalesce(n, 0L)) %>%
  left_join(cat_n, by = "job_category") %>%
  mutate(share = n / cat_jobs,
         cat_label = paste0(str_wrap(job_category, 12), "\n(n = ", cat_jobs, ")"),
         skill_name = factor(skill_name, levels = rev(top_skills)))

ggplot(by_cat, aes(cat_label, skill_name, fill = share)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, 1),
                colour = share > 0.55), size = 2.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "#2b2b2b"), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("#f4f8fe", "#9ec5f4", "#3987e5", "#1c5cab", "#0d366b"),
                       labels = percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  labs(title = "Share of postings in each job category that mention each skill",
       subtitle = "Top 18 skills overall; small categories (n < 15) are noisy",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Share") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9),
        legend.position = "right")
```

Each role has its own profile:

* **AI/ML** postings are associated with Python, Machine Learning, LLMs and
  PyTorch. SQL appears in only `r pct(by_cat$share[by_cat$job_category == "AI/ML" & by_cat$skill_name == "SQL"], 1)`
  of them, far less than in any other category.
* **Data Analytics** and **Business Intelligence** rely most on SQL plus a BI
  tool (Tableau, Power BI), with dbt appearing in about a quarter of analytics
  postings.
* **Data Engineering** combines SQL and Python with data pipelines, dbt, ETL,
  Snowflake, Databricks and cloud platforms.
* **Python and SQL** are the only skills common (≥ 40%) in nearly every
  category.


# Value Proxy 2 — Pay

## Salary by role and seniority

```{r pay-context, fig.height = 4.8}
pay <- pay %>%
  mutate(job_category = fct_reorder(job_category, salary_midpoint_annual, median))

g1 <- ggplot(pay, aes(salary_midpoint_annual, job_category)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#cde2fb", colour = "#184f95", outlier.colour = col_neg,
               width = 0.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "K")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)

(g1) + plot_annotation(
  title = "Advertised salary midpoints by job category",
  theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")))
```

Data Science and AI/ML postings pay the most, Data Analytics and BI the least

* **Skill premium**: median salary of postings that mention the skill minus the
  median of postings that do not, with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval.

Small categories are merged for modeling (Business Intelligence → Data
Analytics; Database → Data Engineering; Statistics → Data Science), and only
skills mentioned in at least 10 salaried postings are estimated.

```{r premiums}
set.seed(607)

pay_model <- pay %>%
  mutate(cat_model = fct_collapse(as.character(job_category),
                                  "Data Analytics"   = c("Data Analytics", "Business Intelligence"),
                                  "Data Engineering" = c("Data Engineering", "Database"),
                                  "Data Science"     = c("Data Science", "Statistics")) %>%
           fct_relevel("Data Analytics"),
         log_salary = log(salary_midpoint_annual))

pay_skills <- skills %>% filter(job_id %in% pay_model$job_id)
eligible <- count(pay_skills, skill_name) %>% filter(n >= 10) %>% pull(skill_name)

boot_median_diff <- function(y, x, reps = 2000) {
  est <- median(y[x]) - median(y[!x])
  b <- replicate(reps, {
    i <- sample(length(y), replace = TRUE)
    yy <- y[i]; xx <- x[i]
    median(yy[xx]) - median(yy[!xx])
  })
  tibble(raw = est, raw_lo = quantile(b, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
         raw_hi = quantile(b, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE))
}

premiums <- map_dfr(eligible, function(s) {
  d <- pay_model %>% mutate(has = job_id %in% pay_skills$job_id[pay_skills$skill_name == s])
  fit <- lm(log_salary ~ has + cat_model, data = d)
  co  <- tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE) %>% filter(term == "hasTRUE")
  bind_cols(
    tibble(skill_name = s, n_with = sum(d$has)),
    boot_median_diff(d$salary_midpoint_annual, d$has),
    tibble(adj = exp(co$estimate) - 1, adj_lo = exp(co$conf.low) - 1,
           adj_hi = exp(co$conf.high) - 1, adj_p = co$p.value)
  )
}) %>%
  left_join(select(demand, skill_name,share), by = "skill_name") %>%
  arrange(desc(adj))

write_csv(premiums, "Data/Analysis/skill_salary_premiums.csv")
```

```{r premium-plot, fig.height = 7.8, fig.width = 10}
order_lvls <- premiums$skill_name[order(premiums$adj)]

raw_plot <- ggplot(premiums, aes(raw, factor(skill_name, levels = order_lvls))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#8a8984") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = raw_lo, xmax = raw_hi), height = 0, colour = "#b9b7b0",
                 linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = raw > 0), size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = col_main, `FALSE` = col_neg), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "K")) +
  labs(x = "USD per year", y = NULL)


(raw_plot) + plot_annotation(
  title = "Salary associated with mentioning each skill",
  subtitle = "Median with − median without",
  theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")))
```

**Findings:**

* **Raw gaps are large and mostly reflect the job type.** Machine Learning,
  LLM and PyTorch postings advertise about \$28K–\$38K more than other
  postings. Excel, Power BI, Tableau and Data Visualization postings advertise
  \$50K–\$68K *less*. 
* SQL shows a *penalty* of \$40K, only because the
  highest-paying category (AI/ML) rarely lists SQL. 
* **Excel, Data Visualization and Power BI stay lower** even within the same
  job category: Excel by `r pct(-premiums$adj[premiums$skill_name == "Excel"], 1)`,
  Data Visualization by `r pct(-premiums$adj[premiums$skill_name == "Data Visualization"], 1)`
  and Power BI by `r pct(-premiums$adj[premiums$skill_name == "Power BI"], 1)`.
  These are the only statistically significant estimates (p < 0.05).
  Postings that emphasize spreadsheets and visualization tend to be
  reporting-focused roles, which pay less than the rest of their category.
* With `r nrow(pay)` salaried postings, most confidence intervals include zero.

## Answer to the research question

There is no single "most valued" skill. The proxies (demand, pay) agree on some skills and disagree on others:

1. **Foundational skills: Python and SQL are the most valued skills by demand and reach**.
2. **Machine Learning is the best all-round skill. Statistics follows**
3. **BI and spreadsheet skills are in demand but not well paid.** Tableau,
   Power BI

# Limitations and future work

* **Representativeness.** The postings come from companies that use specific
  applicant-tracking systems and are concentrated in the US and in tech.
* **Small analytical sample.** The data-role analysis rests on 226 postings
  (`r nrow(pay)` with usable salaries). 
* **Measurement.** Keyword extraction cannot distinguish required from
  preferred skills or detect proficiency.
* **Advertised, not realized, pay.** 
* **Don't take into account seniority**
* **No longitudinal analysis** 
* **No supply and demand comparison.** Did not integrate CV or resume data.
